rule.vbs100.title: Script file could not be checked
rule.vbs100.rationale: The file is a script type that runs VBScript (.vbs, .vbe) or can contain it (.wsf, .wsc, .hta), but it could not be read. Check it manually.
rule.vbs101.title: VBScript file (.vbs)
rule.vbs101.rationale: Windows runs .vbs files with the VBScript engine. Microsoft has deprecated VBScript: it is now a Windows feature on demand that is expected to be disabled by default in a later phase and removed after that. Without VBScript, the file no longer runs.
rule.vbs102.title: Encoded VBScript file (.vbe)
rule.vbs102.rationale: .vbe files contain VBScript that was scrambled with the Script Encoder; Windows runs them with the VBScript engine ("VBScript.Encode"). The encoding does not change the language: without VBScript, the file no longer runs. The affected lines are shown after decoding the file.
rule.vbs103.title: Windows Script File (.wsf) with VBScript
rule.vbs103.rationale: The file contains a script element in VBScript (or VBScript.Encode). Windows Script Host runs it with the VBScript engine, so this part stops working once VBScript is disabled.
rule.vbs104.title: Windows Script Component (.wsc) with VBScript
rule.vbs104.rationale: The script component contains VBScript code. Programs that use the component call the VBScript engine; without VBScript, the component can no longer be used.
rule.vbs105.title: HTML application (.hta) with VBScript
rule.vbs105.rationale: The HTML application contains VBScript (script blocks, event handlers or vbscript: links). mshta.exe runs this code with the VBScript engine; without VBScript, these parts of the application stop working.
rule.vbs200.title: Script or shortcut could not be checked
rule.vbs200.rationale: The file may start VBScript but could not be read or analysed. Check it manually.
rule.vbs201.title: Script starts VBScript
rule.vbs201.rationale: The script runs a VBScript file or VBScript code – through wscript.exe or cscript.exe, by starting a .vbs/.vbe file directly or through a vbscript: command (e.g. with mshta.exe). This call fails once VBScript is disabled.
rule.vbs202.title: Script starts a script whose language is not known
rule.vbs202.rationale: The script starts a Windows Script File (.wsf), an HTML application (.hta) or a script through the Windows Script Host whose language only shows in the started file. Check whether that file uses VBScript.
rule.vbs211.title: Shortcut starts VBScript
rule.vbs211.rationale: The shortcut runs a VBScript file or VBScript code (through wscript.exe, cscript.exe or mshta.exe, or by opening a .vbs/.vbe file). Once VBScript is disabled, the shortcut no longer works.
rule.vbs212.title: Shortcut starts a script whose language is not known
rule.vbs212.rationale: The shortcut starts a .wsf or .hta file or a script through the Windows Script Host whose language only shows in the started file. Check whether that file uses VBScript.
rule.vbs300.title: Task, autostart entry, service or logon script could not be checked
rule.vbs300.rationale: The entry may start VBScript but could not be read or analysed. Check it manually.
rule.vbs301.title: Scheduled task runs VBScript
rule.vbs301.rationale: The task runs a VBScript file or VBScript code automatically. Once VBScript is disabled, the task fails – often unnoticed, because nobody watches its result.
rule.vbs302.title: Scheduled task starts a script whose language is not known
rule.vbs302.rationale: The task starts a .wsf or .hta file or a script through the Windows Script Host whose language only shows in the started file. Check whether that file uses VBScript.
rule.vbs311.title: Autostart entry runs VBScript
rule.vbs311.rationale: The entry (Run/RunOnce key, startup folder, Winlogon or Active Setup) runs VBScript automatically at startup or logon. Once VBScript is disabled, it fails at every logon.
rule.vbs312.title: Autostart entry starts a script whose language is not known
rule.vbs312.rationale: The autostart entry starts a .wsf or .hta file or a script through the Windows Script Host whose language only shows in the started file. Check whether that file uses VBScript.
rule.vbs321.title: Windows service runs VBScript
rule.vbs321.rationale: The service (or its failure command, or a service wrapper such as srvany or NSSM) runs VBScript. Once VBScript is disabled, the service no longer starts or its function fails.
rule.vbs322.title: Windows service starts a script whose language is not known
rule.vbs322.rationale: The service starts a .wsf or .hta file or a script through the Windows Script Host whose language only shows in the started file. Check whether that file uses VBScript.
rule.vbs331.title: WMI event subscription runs VBScript
rule.vbs331.rationale: A permanent WMI event consumer runs VBScript when its event occurs (ActiveScriptEventConsumer with the VBScript engine, or a command-line consumer that starts VBScript). Such subscriptions run invisibly; once VBScript is disabled, they fail. An unknown subscription can also be a sign of compromise.
rule.vbs332.title: WMI event subscription starts a script whose language is not known
rule.vbs332.rationale: A permanent WMI event consumer starts a script whose language only shows in the started file. Check the subscription and the script.
rule.vbs341.title: Logon, logoff, startup or shutdown script runs VBScript
rule.vbs341.rationale: Group Policy or the user's environment runs the script at logon, logoff, startup or shutdown, and it needs VBScript. Once VBScript is disabled, the drive mappings, printer connections or other settings it makes are missing – on every affected computer.
rule.vbs342.title: Logon, logoff, startup or shutdown script whose language is not known
rule.vbs342.rationale: The policy starts a .wsf or .hta file or a script through the Windows Script Host whose language only shows in the started file. Check whether that file uses VBScript.
rule.vbs400.title: Installer package could not be checked
rule.vbs400.rationale: The MSI package could not be read or analysed, so its custom actions are unknown. Check it manually (e.g. with Orca) for VBScript custom actions.
rule.vbs401.title: Installer package runs VBScript (custom action)
rule.vbs401.rationale: The package contains a VBScript custom action (type 6, 22, 38 or 54) that runs during installation, repair, update or removal. Once VBScript is disabled, these operations fail – typically only when they are needed, e.g. at an uninstall or repair.
rule.vbs402.title: Installer package contains a VBScript custom action (impact uncertain)
rule.vbs402.rationale: The package contains a VBScript custom action whose errors are ignored or that is not scheduled in any sequence. The operation does not stop, but whatever the script does is missing. Check what the custom action is for.
rule.vbs500.title: Event log could not be checked
rule.vbs500.rationale: The event log could not be read, so recorded VBScript use is unknown.
rule.vbs501.title: Windows recorded VBScript use
rule.vbs501.rationale: Windows logged a VBScript deprecation alert (event 4096, source VBScriptDeprecationAlert) because this program used VBScript. It is proof of actual use; the process tree shows how it was started.
rule.vbs502.title: Sysmon recorded a VBScript start
rule.vbs502.rationale: Sysmon logged the start of a process that runs VBScript (wscript.exe, cscript.exe or mshta.exe with a VBScript file or vbscript: code). It is proof of actual use; find out what started it.
rule.vbs503.title: Sysmon recorded a program loading the VBScript engine
rule.vbs503.rationale: Sysmon logged that this program loaded vbscript.dll. The program most likely runs VBScript code (e.g. embedded scripts or regular expressions); check what it uses it for.
rule.vbs600.title: Office macro could not be checked
rule.vbs600.rationale: The file can contain VBA macros that could not be read: it needs a password to open, is protected with rights management or damaged, or it stores its macros in a format that is not supported (e.g. Access 97, Excel 5.0/95, web page). Check it manually in Office.
rule.vbs601.title: Macro uses VBScript regular expressions
rule.vbs601.rationale: The VBA project uses the regular expressions of VBScript – through CreateObject("VBScript.RegExp") or a reference to "Microsoft VBScript Regular Expressions" (vbscript.dll). Once VBScript is disabled, this code fails; a missing reference even stops the whole project from compiling. Office Version 2508 (Build 19127.20154) and later include RegExp in VBA itself: remove the reference and use New RegExp.
rule.vbs611.title: Macro runs VBScript code (Script Control, execScript)
rule.vbs611.rationale: The macro runs VBScript code inside Office – through the Microsoft Script Control (MSScriptControl.ScriptControl) or the execScript method of an HTML document window, with the language VBScript. Once VBScript is disabled, this code no longer works.
rule.vbs612.title: Macro runs script code (language not recognisable)
rule.vbs612.rationale: The macro runs script code through the Microsoft Script Control or execScript but sets the language elsewhere or only at run time. Check whether it is VBScript – JScript is not affected.
rule.vbs621.title: Macro starts VBScript
rule.vbs621.rationale: The macro starts a VBScript file (.vbs, .vbe) – through the Windows Script Host (wscript, cscript), directly (e.g. WScript.Shell.Run, ShellExecute) or as vbscript: code. Once VBScript is disabled, the started script no longer runs.
rule.vbs622.title: Macro starts a script of unknown language
rule.vbs622.rationale: The macro starts a Windows Script File (.wsf), an HTML application (.hta), a script component or a script through the Windows Script Host whose language only shows in the started file. Check whether that file uses VBScript.
rule.vbs632.title: Macro uses Windows Script Host objects
rule.vbs632.rationale: The macro creates objects of the Windows Script Host (e.g. WScript.Shell, WScript.Network). Microsoft names calls of .vbs files and the regular expressions of VBScript as affected, not these objects. Check whether the macro uses them to start or read VBScript files.
rule.vbs901.title: Hard-coded credentials
rule.vbs901.rationale: A password, a connection-string password or credentials in a URL are written into the script or its call. Anyone who can read the file can use them. The value was masked and not stored. Move the secret into a protected store when the script is migrated.
hint.rewriteScript: Rewrite the script in PowerShell, the supported successor on Windows. Typical counterparts: WScript.Echo → Write-Output; FileSystemObject → Get-ChildItem, Copy-Item, Get-Content, Set-Content; WScript.Shell Run → Start-Process; GetObject("winmgmts:…") → Get-CimInstance; WScript.Network MapNetworkDrive → New-PSDrive -Persist. Then change every task, shortcut or policy that starts the script (listed as separate findings) and test on a machine without the VBScript feature.
hint.scriptComponent: A Windows Script Component is a COM object written in script. Replace it with a PowerShell module or a small .NET class library, change the programs that create the object (search their code for its ProgID) and unregister the old component afterwards.
hint.htmlApplication: HTML applications run in mshta.exe. Rebuild the tool as a PowerShell script with a Windows Forms or WPF window, or as a small web application. Parts written in JScript keep working; only the VBScript parts stop.
hint.callingScript: Migrate the VBScript file this script starts (listed separately if the scan found it), then change the call to start the PowerShell version, e.g. powershell.exe -NoProfile -File "…\script.ps1".
hint.unknownLanguage: Open the started file and check the language of its script parts: VBScript blocks or .vbs/.vbe files need migrating (see the hints for script files); JScript keeps working.
hint.shortcut: Point the shortcut to the migrated PowerShell script (target: powershell.exe -NoProfile -File "…\script.ps1") or remove it if nobody uses it.
hint.scheduledTask: Migrate the script, then change the task action to powershell.exe with the arguments -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File "…\script.ps1". Check the task's last run result after the change – failing tasks often go unnoticed.
hint.autostart: Migrate the script and point the entry to PowerShell (powershell.exe -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -File "…\script.ps1"). On managed computers, consider moving the entry to Group Policy or Intune.
hint.service: Replace the command of the service or of its wrapper (srvany, NSSM) with the migrated PowerShell script, or rebuild the service in a supported language. Check the service's recovery actions as well.
hint.wmiSubscription: First make sure the subscription is known and wanted – attackers use permanent WMI subscriptions too. Replace a wanted one with a scheduled task with an event trigger that runs PowerShell, then remove the old consumer, filter and binding from root\subscription.
hint.logonScript: Group Policy Preferences map drives and printers and set registry values without any script – often the simplest replacement. For the remaining logic, use the "PowerShell Scripts" tab of the logon or startup script policy.
hint.installerPackage: Ask the vendor for a version without VBScript custom actions. For your own packages, replace the custom action with standard Windows Installer actions or a DLL/EXE custom action (e.g. with WiX). Test install, repair, update and uninstall on a machine without the VBScript feature.
hint.loggedUse: The log proves the use: find the script or program through the process tree and command line, then migrate it as described for its type. The finding shows when the use was logged first and last.
hint.engineLoaded: A program loaded the VBScript engine (vbscript.dll), for example for embedded scripts or VBScript regular expressions. Ask its vendor for a version without VBScript; in your own programs, replace the component (e.g. with .NET regular expressions).
hint.regExp: Office's own alternative: Office Version 2508 (Build 19127.20154) and later include RegExp in VBA. Remove the reference "Microsoft VBScript Regular Expressions 5.5" and create the object with New RegExp instead of CreateObject("VBScript.RegExp"). Older Office versions need another solution, e.g. Like, InStr and Split.
hint.scriptControl: Move the VBScript code into the VBA project itself: VBA is closely related to VBScript, so most statements run unchanged in a VBA module (the Script Control is not available in 64-bit Office anyway). Code that has to stay outside Office can become a PowerShell script started with Shell.
hint.macroStartsScript: Migrate the started VBScript file to PowerShell and start the new file from VBA, e.g. with Shell "powershell.exe -NoProfile -File …" – or move the logic into VBA itself.
hint.wshObjects: Check what the macro does with the object. Office's own alternatives: Shell and Environ$ to start programs and read environment variables, CreateObject("Shell.Application") for folders, Windows API declarations for the rest. Calls that start .vbs files are listed as separate findings.
hint.credentials: Change the password – anyone who could read the file could use it. Keep secrets out of scripts: use the Windows Credential Manager, the PowerShell SecretManagement module or a group Managed Service Account for tasks and services.
hint.notCheckable: Make the item readable and scan again, or check it by hand.
hint.windowsComponent: Part of Windows and maintained by Microsoft – do not change or delete it. Your own scripts, tasks or policies that call these files are listed as separate findings; migrate those calls.
hint.reason.passwordProtected: Open the file with its password and check the VBA project in the editor, or remove the password temporarily and scan again.
hint.reason.accessDenied: Run the collector as administrator or as SYSTEM (e.g. through Group Policy, Intune or your RMM tool) and scan again.
hint.reason.locked: Another program had the file open. Scan again when that program is closed.
hint.reason.corrupt: The file is damaged or has an unexpected format. Open it in the program it belongs to; if it works there, check it by hand.
hint.reason.unsupportedFormat: This format is not read (e.g. Access 97, Excel 5.0/95). Save the file in a current format and scan again, or check it by hand.
hint.reason.tooLarge: The file exceeds the collector's safety limit. Check it by hand, e.g. search it for vbscript, wscript, cscript and .vbs.
hint.reason.cloudPlaceholder: Online-only cloud file – reading it would have downloaded it. Make it available offline ("Always keep on this device") and scan again, or check it where it is stored.
hint.reason.encrypted: The file is encrypted (e.g. with EFS). Scan it as a user who can read it, or check it by hand.
hint.reason.networkLocation: The script is on a network path. Scan that path once with --include-unc from any machine that can read it.
hint.reason.internalError: The analysis failed. Check the item by hand and report the problem to support – the result file contains no content of the item.
setAside.superseded: Older scan – a newer scan of this machine is evaluated
setAside.machineLimit: Not evaluated – beyond the machine limit of the free edition
sourceReason.unreadableItems: Some items could not be read
sourceReason.userHivesNotRead: The registry of some users could not be read
effort.sizeFactor: × {factor} for the size of the script.
effort.typicalScript: Includes a typical script that the scan did not find.
effort.basis.scriptSize: Per script, times a factor for its size (up to 8 KiB × 1, 32 KiB × 2, 128 KiB × 4, larger × 8)

report.title: VBScript dependency assessment
report.subtitle: Management report: risks, priorities and migration effort
report.generatedWith: Created with {product} {version} · rule catalog as of {date}
report.confidential: Confidential: this report contains names and paths of the examined environment. Passwords and other secrets found in scripts were masked by the collector and are not part of it.
report.section.coverage: Coverage and limits of the scan
report.summary.intro_one: The {product} collector examined {count} machine for dependencies on VBScript: script files, scheduled tasks, services, autostart entries, logon scripts, WMI subscriptions, installer packages, event logs and Office macros. This report shows what will stop working, how urgent it is and what the migration may cost.
report.summary.intro_other: The {product} collector examined {count} machines for dependencies on VBScript: script files, scheduled tasks, services, autostart entries, logon scripts, WMI subscriptions, installer packages, event logs and Office macros. This report shows what will stop working, how urgent it is and what the migration may cost.
report.summary.high_one: {count} dependency runs automatically or was demonstrably used, and it will stop working when VBScript is disabled.
report.summary.high_other: {count} dependencies run automatically or were demonstrably used, and they will stop working when VBScript is disabled.
report.summary.noHigh: No dependency that breaks runs automatically or was recorded in an event log.
report.summary.medium_one: {count} further item has medium risk: it breaks when it is used (Office macro, shortcut, installer action) or runs automatically but needs a check.
report.summary.medium_other: {count} further items have medium risk: they break when they are used (Office macros, shortcuts, installer actions) or run automatically but need a check.
report.summary.notCheckable_one: {count} item could not be checked (for example protected, locked or online-only) – see the coverage section.
report.summary.notCheckable_other: {count} items could not be checked (for example protected, locked or online-only) – see the coverage section.
report.summary.credentials_one: {count} script or macro contains a password or other credentials in plain text – change them when migrating.
report.summary.credentials_other: {count} scripts or macros contain passwords or other credentials in plain text – change them when migrating.
report.summary.windows_one: {count} file is part of Windows. Microsoft maintains it; it is listed separately and needs no migration.
report.summary.windows_other: {count} files are part of Windows. Microsoft maintains them; they are listed separately and need no migration.
report.summary.effort: Rule-of-thumb effort for the migration: {min}–{max} hours (about {minDays}–{maxDays} person-days). The effort section explains what is included.
report.summary.coverage: {full} of {machines} machines were scanned without limitations. The scan shows what the collector could read – it does not prove that nothing else depends on VBScript.
report.summary.timeline: Timeline: Microsoft has deprecated VBScript. In the next phase – expected around 2027 – it is to be disabled by default, and removed later. Source: {publisher}, “{title}” (published {published}, checked {checked}). Microsoft may change these dates.
report.risks.intro: The risk combines how a dependency runs with how certain the impact is. High: breaks and runs automatically (scheduled tasks, services, autostart, logon scripts, WMI) or was recorded in an event log. Medium: breaks when it is used (Office macros, shortcuts, installer actions), or runs automatically but needs a check. Low: files without a known trigger and items that need a check.
report.nothingFound: Nothing found: the evaluated result files contain no dependency on VBScript.
report.priorities.intro_one: The most urgent item. The technical Excel list contains every item with all its locations.
report.priorities.intro_other: The {count} most urgent items, in the order of risk. The technical Excel list contains every item with all its locations.
report.priorities.more_one: {count} more item is listed in the technical Excel list.
report.priorities.more_other: {count} more items are listed in the technical Excel list.
report.recommendations.intro: One recommendation per kind of dependency; the numbers refer to the priorities and the technical list. {product} never changes or converts code – the migration itself is done by people.
report.effort.intro: All figures in this section are rules of thumb – rough ranges for planning, not a quote. They are based on typical cases per rule and on the size of the scripts; the actual effort depends on what the scripts do, on testing and on how changes are rolled out.
report.effort.assumption.perRule: Each rule has a range in hours for a typical case. Larger scripts count more: up to 8 KiB × 1, up to 32 KiB × 2, up to 128 KiB × 4, larger × 8.
report.effort.assumption.central: Items found on several machines are counted once – the change is assumed to be rolled out centrally (Group Policy, Intune or an RMM tool).
report.effort.assumption.copies: Identical copies of a file are counted once. An entry whose script the scan did not find includes the effort of a typical script, once per script.
report.effort.assumption.windows: Windows components are not counted: Microsoft maintains them.
report.effort.assumption.excluded: Not included: project management, approvals, training, rollout to machines without central management and troubleshooting in production.
report.coverage.intro: No completeness promise: the report covers what the collector could read on the evaluated machines at the time of the scan. Event logs only reach back as far as shown below (Windows overwrites old entries), protected or locked items are listed as not checkable, network paths were only read where explicitly requested, and machines that were not scanned are not included.
report.coverage.machines: {full} of {machines} machines were scanned without limitations, {limited} with limitations.
report.coverage.deprecation: VBScript deprecation alerts (Application log, event 4096) could be read on {read} of {reported} machines; the logs reached back {minDays} to {maxDays} days (oldest entry: {earliest}).
report.coverage.deprecationNone: No machine reported readable VBScript deprecation alerts (Application log, event 4096).
report.coverage.sysmon: Sysmon (process starts and loads of vbscript.dll) could be read on {read} of {reported} machines.
report.coverage.files: File scan: {entries} entries examined, {errors} could not be read, {skipped} were deliberately not examined (links, online-only cloud folders).
report.coverage.setAside_one: {count} result file was not evaluated: an older scan of an evaluated machine, or beyond the edition's machine limit (see the technical list).
report.coverage.setAside_other: {count} result files were not evaluated: older scans of evaluated machines, or beyond the edition's machine limit (see the technical list).
report.coverage.notCheckable: Items that could not be checked, by reason
report.windows.intro: These files belong to Windows: they are in the component store (WinSxS), have the same content as a file there, are Windows data such as the User Access Logging databases, or are part of a Windows container image. Microsoft maintains them – they need no migration. Your own scripts, tasks or policies that call them are listed as separate findings.
report.windows.more_one: {count} more Windows component is listed in the technical Excel list.
report.windows.more_other: {count} more Windows components are listed in the technical Excel list.
report.method.classification: Every finding comes from a rule of the rule catalog. “Breaks” means the item stops working when VBScript is disabled – backed by the sources listed below. “Review” means the item may be affected and needs a manual check; items that could not be checked are always “review”.
report.method.risk: Risk and priority: automatic execution first, then use recorded in an event log, Office macros, programs started by users, installer actions and files without a known trigger; within each, “breaks” before “review”. A script that a task, service or policy starts counts like that entry.
report.method.dedup: Merging: the newest scan of each machine is evaluated. The same file on a network share seen from several machines, and the same entry or identical file on several machines, is listed once with all its machines.
report.method.windows: Windows components are recognised by their location (component store, User Access Logging databases, Windows folders of container images) or by identical content – never by their file name alone.
report.powershell.intro: Common VBScript objects and statements with their PowerShell counterparts – a starting point for rewriting scripts by hand. {product} never converts code.
report.freeNotice: Free edition: finding list for up to {max} machines, without migration hints, effort estimates and PDF report. A license adds them.
report.rowsLeftOut_one: {count} more row does not fit into one Excel sheet.
report.rowsLeftOut_other: {count} more rows do not fit into one Excel sheet.

collector.banner: {product} Collector {version} – read-only scan for VBScript dependencies
collector.help:
Usage: {program} [options]

Scans this computer for VBScript dependencies and writes one result file.
Nothing on the computer is changed and no network connection is made.

Options:
  --out <file or folder>  Where to write the result file. Default: the current
                          folder, named <computer>_<date-time>.{extension}.
                          Existing files are never overwritten.
  --path <folder>         Scan only this local folder instead of all local
                          drives (repeatable).
  --include-unc <\\server\share\folder>
                          Also scan this network path, with the rights of the
                          running account (repeatable). Network paths are never
                          scanned otherwise.
  --files-only            Scan files only; skip the registry, scheduled tasks,
